findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: SCAPE discount rate increase has suspended critical pension calculations pending new actuarial factors, extending timelines by up to six months
findings.detail: The SCAPE discount rate increased from CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0% effective 19 May 2026. This has required suspension of non-Club transfers, aggregation calculations, and divorce cash equivalent valuations until updated actuarial factors are issued. Early and late retirement factors are expected within six weeks, with remaining factors issued over six months.
findings.matters: Suspended transfer-out processing creates bottlenecks affecting member and employer experience; delays in member valuations disrupt retirement planning for members and inter-fund administration
findings.figures: Discount rate increase: CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0%; factor delays: 6 weeks to 6 months
findings.quote: The revised SCAPE discount rate applies from 19 May 2026 and has increased from CPI + 1.7% to CPI + 2.0%. As a result, we had to suspend some calculations until new factors are issued. These include certain non-Club transfers and aggregation calculations, as well as all cash equivalent values (CEVs) for divorce.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: Internal audit rated life certificate controls as only partially effective, finding multiple risks not effectively managed
findings.detail: Bradford's Internal Audit team audited life certificate administration and determined that the control environment is only partially effective. Multiple examined risks were found to not be effectively managed, and the audit concluded that controls would benefit from significant improvement to support key business objectives. Three recommendations were made and implemented.
findings.matters: Weakness in life certificate controls creates risk of overpayments to deceased pensioners; as a material process in pension administration, control failures here expose Bradford to financial loss and regulatory scrutiny
findings.figures: Three audit recommendations made and implemented
findings.quote: It is audit's opinion that the standard of control of identified risks in the system is partially effective. The audit review has determined that a number of the risks examined are not effectively managed. The control environment would benefit from significant improvement to support the achievement of key business objectives.

findings.committee: West Yorkshire Pension Fund Advisory Panel
findings.paper_title: Agenda item 8 Pensions Administration Report
findings.headline: WYPF will breach McCloud statutory guidance by failing to complete retrospective pension amendments by 31 August 2026
findings.detail: The McCloud implementation statutory guidance requires all retrospective amendments to members' pensions to be concluded by 31 August 2026. Civica, the pensions administration system provider, has not delivered the necessary software development to enable retrospective calculations. As a result, WYPF will be in breach of the guidance and must report this to the Pensions Regulator. The formal recommendation is that this breach is reported to TPR.
findings.matters: Breaching Pensions Regulator requirements can result in fines and regulatory action; as Bradford hosts WYPF, this compliance failure reflects on Bradford's governance and ability to manage complex regulatory obligations
findings.figures: Deadline 31 August 2026; software update still not received as of report date (27 August 2026)
findings.quote: The McCloud implementation statutory guidance states that all retrospective amendments to members' pensions should be concluded by 31 August 2026. Civica clients have not received the software development to enable them to do the retrospective calculations. As a result WYPF will be in breach of the guidance and should report this to the Pensions Regulator ('TPR').

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: New five-tier business rates multiplier system sharply reduces rates for retail, hospitality and leisure from April 2026
findings.detail: From April 2026, five new multiplier rate bands replaced the previous two-tier system. Rates for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses were substantially cut: small business multiplier fell from 49.9p to 38.2p (23% reduction); standard RHL from 55.5p to 43.0p (23% reduction). This follows a simultaneous property revaluation, compounding revenue reduction.
findings.matters: Substantial reduction in multiplier rates for economically distressed business sectors reduces projected business rates income and creates budgetary pressure in the forward year.
findings.figures: Small Business RHL: 49.9p (2025/26) → 38.2p (2026/27); Standard RHL: 55.5p → 43.0p
findings.quote: In April 2026, five multiplier rates were introduced, replacing the two that existed, as shown in the Table below... Small Business (retail, hospitality and leisure) Below £51,000 38.2; Standard (non retail, hospitality and leisure) £51,000 to £499,999 43.0

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Successful business rates appeals created £2.96m budget hit in single financial year
findings.detail: In 2025/26, successful appeals against rateable values resulted in retrospective adjustments totalling £2.96m. These adjustments can be backdated over several years and have material impact on the council's budget position. The council manages this through provisions in its budget process but volatility reduces predictability.
findings.matters: Large appeals-driven revenue adjustments create unpredictability in the council's tax income and require reserve provisions to absorb impacts; this reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £2.96m in retrospective adjustments in 2025/26; adjustments can be backdated over several years
findings.quote: In 2025/26, successful appeals by businesses have resulted in retrospective adjustments in liability totalling £2.96m.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Council tax collection rate fell to 93.54% following 9.99% tax increase
findings.detail: In-year council tax collection declined from 94.04% to 93.54% in 2025/26 despite a 9.99% council tax rise that increased the total liability from £308m to £341m. The paper attributes collection difficulties to the large tax increase, new charges on empty properties from April 2025, and poverty affecting residents' ability to pay.
findings.matters: A large tax increase producing a collection rate decline rather than improvement indicates residents are reaching the limit of affordability; this signals underlying financial stress and suggests collection will remain difficult.
findings.figures: Council Tax liability 2025/26: £341m; 2024/25: £308m (increase of £33m or 10.7%); 9.99% council tax rise; collection rate fell to 93.54% from 94.04%
findings.quote: Council Tax in year collection for 2025/26 was 93.54% which is 0.5% down on the previous year (Table 4) Factors affecting collection include the 9.99% Council Tax rise in 2025/26, increases in charges on empty properties which came into force in April 2025 and wider factors affecting collection such as poverty in the district.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Business rates collection rate declined to 95.28%, lowest in five-year trend
findings.detail: In-year business rates collection fell from 96.45% in 2024/25 to 95.28% in 2025/26—a drop of 1.17 percentage points. The paper attributes this to increased collection amounts (£138m vs £128m), reduced reliefs, and ongoing economic pressures particularly affecting retail, hospitality and leisure businesses.
findings.matters: Declining collection efficiency reduces cash available to the council and indicates collection effort is not keeping pace with growing arrears; this impacts cash flow and financial planning.
findings.figures: 2025/26 collection: 95.28%; 2024/25: 96.45%; 2023/24: 97.26%—a three-year downward trend
findings.quote: Business Rates in year collection for 2025/26 was 95.28% which is 1.17% down on the previous year (Table 1). Factors affecting collection include the increased amount to collect, decreases in reliefs and the ongoing economic situation which affects businesses (particularly the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors).

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Outstanding business rates arrears more than doubled to £5.3m whilst 463 businesses face insolvency or strike-off
findings.detail: Business rates debt outstanding at end March 2026 reached £5.336m, doubling from £2.851m a year earlier. This occurs amid 350 companies identified at proposal to strike-off stage and 113 in liquidation, administration or insolvency, indicating acute economic distress in the local business environment affecting payment capacity.
findings.matters: Doubling of business rates arrears combined with high insolvency rates indicates the local business base is under severe stress; this threatens future collection and reflects economic deterioration affecting the council's revenue base.
findings.figures: Outstanding debt 2025/26: £5,336k vs 2024/25: £2,851k; 350 companies at proposal to strike off; 113 in insolvency/administration/liquidation
findings.quote: Active Business Rates data is matched to Company House records monthly, and the latest report shows that there are 350 cases at proposal to strike off and 113 cases identified where the ratepayer is in liquidation, administration or other form of insolvency.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Business Rates and Council Tax Collection
findings.headline: Outstanding council tax arrears doubled year-on-year to £20.6m
findings.detail: Council tax debt outstanding at end March 2026 reached £20.591m, more than double the £9.949m owed a year earlier. This £10.6m increase in arrears in a single year signals rapidly deteriorating payment discipline among residents despite the council's collection activities including automated reminders and payment arrangements.
findings.matters: Doubling of council tax arrears in one year indicates severe and worsening payment difficulties among residents and threatens council cash flow; this affects financial stability and signals economic stress in the district.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £20,591k outstanding; 2024/25: £9,949k outstanding; in-year collection rate fell from 96.14% to 93.54%
findings.quote: Table 6 - Council Tax Eventual Collection Rates by year: Outstanding Debt at end March 2026 £000's 2025/26 20,591 Collection rate % 93.54; 2024/25 9,949 96.14

findings.paper_title: DOC J - Exceptions to Financial Regulations Applied During 2025-26 for GAC July 2026 Chair's Brief v3
findings.headline: Exception forms for Respite Home (£0.8m) and Infrastructure Works (£0.2m) redacted on crime prevention grounds
findings.detail: Two of ten exception forms totalling £1m were not published. The council redacted them on grounds of preventing crime and maintaining confidentiality, saying public interest in non-disclosure outweighs public interest in disclosure.
findings.matters: Redaction of governance documents on security grounds raises questions about crime or safety issues affecting capital projects and limits transparency on material capital decisions.
findings.figures: £0.8m and £0.2m (£1m total)
findings.quote: The exception forms relating to Respite Home and Infrastructure Works have been classified as not for publication (NFP) and have therefore been excluded from this report. The information has been redacted on the grounds of prevention of crime, where the public interest in maintaining the exemption is considered to outweigh the public interest in disclosure.

findings.paper_title: DOC J - Exceptions to Financial Regulations Applied During 2025-26 for GAC July 2026 Chair's Brief v3
findings.headline: Mountain View Wall Collapse required emergency £0.3m capital approval
findings.detail: An unplanned structural failure (wall collapse) at Mountain View required emergency capital approval outside normal budget processes, classified as urgent and unable to wait for scheduled budget reporting.
findings.matters: Unexpected infrastructure failures that force emergency funding indicate asset condition issues and unplanned capital pressures on the council.
findings.quote: Mountain View Wall Collapse - £0.3m

findings.paper_title: DOC J - Exceptions to Financial Regulations Applied During 2025-26 for GAC July 2026 Chair's Brief v3
findings.headline: Ten capital projects totalling £4.3m approved as emergency exceptions outside normal budget process in 2025-26
findings.detail: The interim finance officer approved capital expenditure of £4.3m via exception to Financial Regulation 5.31, rather than waiting for scheduled budget reports to Executive. All were classified as urgent and unable to await normal budget processes. Projects included emergency repairs (wall collapse, property adaptations), school improvements, and planned replacements (waste fleet).
findings.matters: Material emergency capital spending outside planned programmes indicates the council faces significant unforecastable capital pressures, asset condition issues, or capital planning constraints that require urgent funding decisions.
findings.figures: £4.3m total: Respite Home £0.8m, Mountain View Wall Collapse £0.3m, Waste/Fleet Replacement Programme £1.4m, Crossflatts and Eldwick Primary Schools £0.6m, Property Programme £0.5m, Ilkley Manor House Re-Roofing £0.2m, Scholemoor Cemetery Drainage £0.2m, Foster Carer Adaption £0.05m, Adult Social Care & Health Urgent Property Adaptions £0.05m, Infrastructure Works £0.2m
findings.quote: In all cases the approval of the projects was determined as urgent in nature and not able to await the next scheduled budget report to Executive.

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: The council emerged from a financial crisis in 2023 (Best Value Notice) but rapid change has created gaps in governance policy compliance.
findings.detail: The auditors note the council 'faced in 2023 which resulted in a Best Value Notice' and 'put an improvement programme in place.' The Notice was withdrawn after 1 year. However, 'a large number of internal audit reports identified material gaps in, and/or non-compliance with, policies and procedures,' which the auditors assess 'partly reflects the scale of the challenges the council is facing which is requiring action at a faster pace than changes in governance and internal control.'
findings.matters: The council's rapid operational and systems change post-crisis, while showing improvement, has left material policy compliance gaps. This is a known risk factor for ongoing control failure or relapse.
findings.figures: Best Value Notice issued 2023, withdrawn after 1 year (2024)
findings.quote: A key context for the thematic issues outlined below has been the Council's approach to addressing the significant financial crisis it faced in 2023 which resulted in a 'Best Value Notice'... [resulting in] a large number of internal audit reports identified material gaps in, and/or non-compliance with, policies and procedures.

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: Accounts Collection control audit was rated ineffective, with six high-priority recommendations for income-related controls.
findings.detail: The Accounts Collection audit received an 'Ineffective' rating with 6 recommendations, all classified as high-priority. This audit examines the council's control over collecting money owed to it.
findings.matters: Ineffective accounts collection controls directly affect the council's revenue position and cash flow, and may indicate broader issues with billing, debt management, or financial processes.
findings.figures: 6 recommendations, 6 high-priority
findings.quote: Accounts Collection [Ineffective] 18/02/2026 6 5

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: Health & Safety audits at corporate and service levels were rated ineffective or partially effective, with 23 of the council's recommendations falling in this category.
findings.detail: Three health and safety audits were conducted: Health & Safety Corporate (Ineffective, 2 high-priority recommendations), Health & Safety - Trees (Partially Effective, 10 of 11 high-priority), and Health & Safety - Playgrounds (Partially Effective, 11 of 12 high-priority). Together these represent 25 recommendations, with 21 classified as high-priority.
findings.matters: Ineffective health and safety controls create operational and liability risk, and may indicate broader governance failures if corporate-level H&S is failing to cascade controls effectively.
findings.figures: H&S Corporate: Ineffective, 2 high-priority; H&S Trees: Partially Effective, 11 recommendations (10 high-priority); H&S Playgrounds: Partially Effective, 12 recommendations (11 high-priority)
findings.quote: Health & Safety Corporate [Ineffective] 24/02/2026 2 2; Health & Safety - Trees [Partially Effective] 21/05/2026 11 10; Health & Safety - Playgrounds [Partially Effective] 12/02/2026 12 11

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: Only 52% of 141 previous internal audit recommendations have been closed; 24% are overdue and 16% have not progressed.
findings.detail: The council reviewed 141 actions from the previous internal audit action tracker. Only 74 (52%) were closed. Of the 67 remaining: 34 (24%) are overdue (not implemented by the agreed action date), 37 (26%) are partially complete, 23 (16%) have not progressed, and 7 (5%) are no longer relevant. The auditors note this reflects 'significant change in personnel, systems and processes' and 'changes in officer roles and responsibilities has interrupted lines of accountability.'
findings.matters: Slow or stalled implementation of audit recommendations indicates weak governance follow-through and management accountability — a leading indicator of sustained control weakness and potential material issues being unresolved.
findings.figures: 52% closed (74 of 141); 24% overdue (34 of 141); 16% no progress (23 of 141)
findings.quote: Of the 67 remaining actions, 23 (16%) have not progressed, 37 (26%) are partially complete and 7 (5%) are no longer relevant... Analysis of the 60 relevant remaining actions shows that 34 (24%) are overdue (not implemented by the agreed action date)

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: Contract management controls were found ineffective across three separate departments: Corporate Procurement, Corporate Resources, and Place.
findings.detail: Three dedicated contract management audits — for Corporate Procurement, Corporate Resources, and Place — all received an 'Ineffective' rating. These three audits generated 31 of the 218 total recommendations (14% of all recommendations), with 29 classified as high-priority.
findings.matters: Ineffective contract management across procurement and major service departments creates direct risk of overspend, non-compliance with terms, and loss of value for money — critical for lenders assessing financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Contract Management - Corporate Procurement: 10 recommendations, 10 high-priority; Corporate Resources: 9 recommendations, 8 high-priority; Place: 12 recommendations, 11 high-priority
findings.quote: Contract Management - Corporate Procurement [Ineffective] 27/06/2025 10 10; Contract Management - Corporate Resources [Ineffective] 24/07/2025 9 8; Contract Management - Place [Ineffective] 25/07/2025 12 11

findings.paper_title: DOC L - City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council - 2025-26 Annual Audit Report FINAL
findings.headline: Six audit reports (17%) concluded internal controls were ineffective, with 69% of all recommendations classified as high-priority.
findings.detail: The council completed 36 internal audit reviews. Six reached an 'ineffective' conclusion on control arrangements. Across all 36 reports, 150 of 218 recommendations (69%) were classified as high-priority. The auditors attribute this to 'the scale of the challenges the council is facing which is requiring action at a faster pace than changes in governance and internal control,' describing it as a 'temporary position' where 'underlying internal control arrangements remain sufficient.'
findings.matters: A 17% failure rate on internal control audits, combined with an unusually high proportion of high-priority findings, indicates material governance gaps that could affect financial management and operational risk.
findings.figures: 6 of 36 reports (17%) ineffective; 150 of 218 recommendations (69%) high-priority
findings.quote: 6 of the 36 (17%) internal audit reports issued reached an 'ineffective' conclusion on internal control arrangements and, of the 218 recommendations made across 36 audit reports, 150 (69%) were classified as 'high priority.'

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Over 72% of external borrowing is fixed-rate PWLB loans, averaging 4.9% interest, maturing 2025-2072
findings.detail: The council's debt structure is predominantly PWLB (Public Works Loan Board) fixed-rate borrowing, with 72% of borrowing at fixed rates. Average interest rate is 4.9%, with maturity profile spread across 47 years. This provides certainty and low refinancing risk over the medium term.
findings.matters: Fixed-rate, long-tenor PWLB borrowing at sub-5% rates is favourable debt structure for a council in financial recovery. However, Bradford's high debt levels (largely driven by Capitalisation Direction) mean absolute debt servicing costs remain elevated.
findings.figures: >72% PWLB fixed-rate; 4.9% average interest rate; maturity 2025-2072
findings.quote: Most external borrowing (over 72%) is fixed rate loans from the Public Works Loan Board, averaging 4.9% interest rates and repayable between 2025 and 2072.

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: PWLB refinancing benefit: new borrowing at 4.45% vs. 6.1% average on maturing debt
findings.detail: The council refinanced £56.483m of maturing PWLB loans that carried an average interest rate of 6.1% with new borrowing of £50m at an average rate of 4.45%. This represents 165 basis points of interest rate benefit on the new debt, though on a lower principal amount.
findings.matters: Interest rate management is material to a council in deficit recovery. The 165 bps saving on new borrowing is significant. However, the lower new borrowing (£50m vs. £56.5m maturing) suggests either deliberate deleveraging or inability to refinance the full amount.
findings.figures: Maturing debt: £56.483m at 6.1% average rate; New borrowing: £50m at 4.45% average rate; Saving: ~165 bps
findings.quote: £56.483m PWLB (Public Works Loan Board) loans matured in 2025-26 with an average rate of interest of 6.1%. New PWLB borrowing undertaken during the year was £50m with an average interest rate of 4.45%.

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Pension liabilities improving in both teachers' discretionary and Local Government Scheme
findings.detail: Net pension liability in teachers' discretionary scheme fell from £47.183m to £44.608m. LGF scheme liability improved from £25.338m to £23.468m. Both schemes show improvement due to better-than-expected asset performance and actuarial gains on liability valuation.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are the council's largest long-term obligation. Improvement through asset performance rather than contribution increases is favourable. However, these are snapshots; ongoing actuarial risk remains.
findings.quote: At end of 2025-26, there is a net pensions liabilities of £44.608m (£47.183m net liability in 2024-25) in teachers' discretionary pension scheme, and a net pension liability of £23.468m in LGF schemes (£25.338m net liability in 2024-25).

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Usable reserves increased by £73.5m to £321.3m as council rebuilds financial resilience
findings.detail: Usable reserves grew from £247.8m (31 March 2025) to £321.3m (31 March 2026), a 29.6% increase. This reverses years of reserve depletion that occurred during the period of structural deficit. The council explicitly states its policy is to build a prudent General Fund working balance to ensure financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's buffer against demand volatility and unexpected costs. Reserve rebuild is a prerequisite for sustainable exit from intervention. Growth of this magnitude is material to credit position.
findings.quote: Useable reserves totalled £321.3m (£247.8m at 31/3/2025). This balance represents a combination of: Funds earmarked for revenue or capital projects... Working balances maintained to cover contingencies... Monies held on behalf of schools

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 materially strengthens medium-term funding outlook with 47.1% Core Spending Power growth
findings.detail: The government's first multi-year funding settlement in over a decade implements Fair Funding Review 2.0, recalculating Baseline Funding Levels using updated Relative Needs Formulas to better reflect need and deprivation. Bradford's Core Spending Power will increase 47.1% between 2024-25 and 2028-29, the 2nd highest of all Metropolitan Districts and 11th highest nationally.
findings.matters: Bradford has been systematically underfunded relative to its need (43.3% ethnic minorities, high deprivation, 42.8% child poverty). Fair Funding 2.0 redirects funding to councils with higher need. This is structural improvement, not one-off grant.
findings.figures: 47.1% Core Spending Power growth 2024-25 to 2028-29; 2nd highest of Metropolitan Districts; 11th highest nationally
findings.quote: Bradford's Core Spending Power will increase by 47.1% between 2024-25 and 2028-29, the 2nd highest of all Metropolitan Districts (MD) and 11th highest nationally.

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Best Value Notice lifted after one year, signalling rapid financial recovery
findings.detail: The council received a Best Value Notice on 29 February 2024 for serious financial concerns. It was lifted on 27 February 2025 after an unprecedentedly brief one-year duration. Independent CIPFA review commended the council's governance improvements and financial control, confirming the scale of the challenge and the realism of the recovery route map.
findings.matters: Best Value intervention is the most visible form of financial distress for councils. Early lifting suggests genuine progress on governance, leadership capability and financial control rather than temporary symptom relief. CIPFA's external validation is credible.
findings.figures: Intervention duration: 12 months (29 February 2024 – 27 February 2025)
findings.quote: The Best Value Notice was lifted on 27 February 2025 after an unprecedentedly brief one-year duration in recognition of the positive progress that the Council is making

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Business Rates collection missed target, falling from 96.45% to 95.28%
findings.detail: Collection rate deteriorated by 117 basis points and fell below the 96% target. Combined with Council Tax underperformance, this signals softer collection performance across both revenue streams.
findings.matters: Business Rates are volatile and harder to recover than Council Tax. Deterioration suggests business distress in the district or billing/collection inefficiency. Either indicates weaker local economic conditions or administrative weakness.
findings.quote: The Business Rates collection rate was 95.28% (96.45% in 24/25), against a target rate of 96%.

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate declined from 94.04% to 93.54%
findings.detail: Collection performance deteriorated by 50 basis points year-on-year. The council aims to recover to 94% in 2026-27 but is currently below 2024-25 outturn. This is the second income-collection metric to deteriorate (see Business Rates).
findings.matters: Council Tax collection is a leading indicator of household financial stress in the district and a direct income loss to the council. Deterioration alongside rising deprivation suggests debt servicing pressures across the local population.
findings.quote: The Council Tax collection rate was 93.54% (94.04% in 2024/25), and we aim to improve this to 94% in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Children's social care identified as persistent cost driver requiring agency staff and residential placements
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies rising cost of residential placements for looked-after children, the number of children still needing care, and spend on agency staff as the key drivers of its financial position. These are demand-led pressures occurring at a time when deprivation (42.8% child poverty, 12th most deprived district nationally) concentrates demand in Bradford.
findings.matters: Children's social care is notoriously difficult to control once children enter the system. Bradford Children and Families Trust is working to address this, but the underlying demographic and deprivation factors will persist. Lenders need visibility on whether cost growth is stabilising.
findings.figures: 42.8% of children in relative poverty (vs. 26% UK-wide); 52,000 children living in poverty; Bradford has 26.3% of West Yorkshire's under-16 population but 32% of its child poverty
findings.quote: the key driver for the Council's financial position was the increasing cost of residential placements for looked after children, the number of children still needing to be in care and spend on agency staff which are all areas BCFT are working to address

findings.paper_title: Doc C - Financial Statements 2025-26 (unaudited) - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council exiting financial intervention two years ahead of schedule
findings.detail: Bradford was originally forecast to need Capitalisation Direction (exceptional support) until 2029-30 (seven years from initial structural deficit identification). Fair Funding 2.0 implementation combined with council's cost control has shortened this to an anticipated exit in 2026-27. The cumulative Capitalisation Direction requirement reduced from £570m to £391m, a saving of £179m.
findings.matters: Early exit from intervention materially improves credit quality and repayment capacity. It demonstrates that the underlying financial weakness is being addressed, not merely masked by temporary support.
findings.figures: £570m forecast → £391m (£179m reduction); exit now 2026-27 vs. 2028-29 forecast
findings.quote: The Council anticipates it will come out of financial intervention during 2026-27 rather than 2028-29, an improvement of 2 years, subject to continued delivery of the improvement plan.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Annual Treasury Management Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital financing costs at 15.3% of net revenue income; report states affordability 'remains a priority'
findings.detail: Debt servicing (MRP, interest, PFI payments) consumes about 15% of available revenue, with medium-term expectation around 14%. The report describes affordability as 'a priority' and notes improvement depends on reducing the capital programme or generating asset sales—both potentially difficult.
findings.matters: At 15% of revenue, capital financing is a significant drag on operating flexibility; the language about affordability being a priority signals concern, and remedies (asset sales, programme cuts) carry delivery risk.
findings.figures: Ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream: 15.3% (2025-26 actual) vs 15.4% (2024-25); expected medium-term 14%
findings.quote: capital financing charges (loan interest, MRP, finance and PFI payments) remains around 15% of net income receivable for the current year... affordability remains a priority.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Annual Treasury Management Report 25-26
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from other councils increased from £149m to £161m to avoid high PWLB rates; council explicitly states this will increase interest costs in 2026-27
findings.detail: Facing PWLB rates ranging from 4.25% to 6.43%, the council shifted £12m additional borrowing to short-term loans from other local authorities. The report flags that this creates higher interest costs, already factored into 2026-27 budgets, signalling anticipated financial pressure.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing creates refinancing risk and operational cost; explicit acknowledgement of higher costs ahead in published budget signals constrained finances.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities: £161.0m (2026) vs £149.0m (2025), an increase of £12.0m
findings.quote: Increased short term borrowing in 2025-26 will mean higher interest costs which has been included in the 2026-27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Annual Treasury Management Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital programme underspend of £59.9m, with General Fund £44.9m below budget, rolling forward to future years
findings.detail: Planned capital expenditure of £279.7m was underspent at £219.8m. The report notes this is due to timing uncertainty in construction schemes, and underspends will move into future years. This suggests delivery challenges or project delays.
findings.matters: Underspends indicate either project slippage or slower delivery; rolled-forward spending extends the financing requirement and defers cost recovery, tightening future affordability.
findings.figures: Total variance to original budget: £59.9m (General Fund £44.9m, HRA £1.0m, Capitalisation Direction £14.0m)
findings.quote: Underspends on Service General Fund Capital budgets will move into next year and beyond. With capital schemes there is a degree of uncertainty to the actual timing of capital spend due to the development of the specific projects.

findings.paper_title: Doc E - Annual Treasury Management Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased to £1,163.2m; £265.9m of this is temporarily covered by reserves rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: The CFR (measure of unfinanced capital expenditure and underlying indebtedness) has grown significantly from £1,078.5m to £1,163.2m. To manage this without incurring higher interest costs, the council is borrowing temporarily from its own cash reserves. This strategy buys time but is not sustainable as reserves will deplete.
findings.matters: Growing CFR signals accumulating capital commitments and indebtedness; using reserves to defer formal borrowing is temporary and eventual external borrowing at current or higher rates will be more expensive.
findings.figures: CFR: £1,163.2m (2026) vs £1,078.5m (2025); under-borrowing position of £265.9m funded from reserves
findings.quote: the Council's underlying need to borrow, that is capital spend funded by borrowing (Capital Financing Requirement) has increased to £1,163.2m, but the Council's actual borrowing has not changed significantly. This is the result of the borrowing strategy where £265.9m has temporarily been borrowed from cash held in earmarked reserves, therefore reducing interest payments.

findings.paper_title: AC - CBMDC Audit Strategy Memorandum 2025-26
findings.headline: Bradford may not have a capitalisation direction in place for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The auditors have identified an enhanced risk that the Council does not have a capitalisation direction from the Secretary of State for 2025/26. If the direction is absent, this would require additional disclosures in the financial statements and potentially an emphasis of matter in the audit report. The auditor will need to confirm with management whether the direction has been obtained.
findings.matters: Capitalisation directions allow councils to treat revenue expenditure as capital, deferring the budget impact. Uncertainty about whether Bradford has one for 2025/26 signals potential revenue budget pressure and raises questions about whether the council has sought exceptional financial support.
findings.figures: No specific amounts disclosed, but this is identified as an audit risk requiring investigation.
findings.quote: There is a risk the Council does not have a capitalisation direction in place for 2025/26, leading to further disclosures in the accounts and an emphasis of matter in the audit report.

findings.paper_title: AD - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Supported Housing Improvement Programme funding status unknown for 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: Supported accommodation management is 'partially externally funded via the Supported Housing Improvement Programme'. The council flags uncertainty: 'it is not known if funding will continue into 2026/27. There may be a need to restructure and resource this going forward to limit the impact on service users'.
findings.matters: Loss of external funding could force unbudgeted costs onto already constrained revenue budget with vulnerable service user population at risk
findings.figures: Funding status unknown beyond 2025/26; restructuring may be required
findings.quote: Management of supported accommodation currently in place is partially externally funded via the Supported Housing Improvement Programme. However, it is not known if funding will continue into 2026/27

findings.paper_title: AD - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: New Choices trading company must be retended or brought back in-house by February 2027
findings.detail: New Choices Ltd, a local authority trading company providing day services to 283 people with disabilities, made a small loss in 2025/26. The council is actively seeking to retender the service; if retender fails, the council must bring services back in-house by 1 February 2027, creating direct cost absorption.
findings.matters: Failed trading arm forces council to either find private-sector buyer or absorb multi-million annual operating cost; either outcome creates budget pressure or commercial risk
findings.figures: 283 service users; 189 staff; small loss recorded 2025/26; retender deadline 1 February 2027
findings.quote: Should this retender be unsuccessful then the services provided by New Choices will be brought back in house by the Council

findings.paper_title: AD - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Children's services hold 'inadequate' Ofsted rating pending full inspection judgment
findings.detail: Bradford has an 'inadequate' Ofsted rating for children's services. A full ILACS inspection was completed in January 2026 with judgment pending. External auditors identified this as a significant weakness: 'the continued inadequate rating and government intervention is evidence of a remaining significant weakness in arrangements'.
findings.matters: Inadequate rating in a major spending area signals delivery failure and heightened government intervention risk; reputational and operational impact likely
findings.figures: ILACS inspection completed January 2026; judgment date unspecified
findings.quote: the continued 'inadequate' rating and government intervention is evidence of a remaining significant weakness in arrangements

findings.paper_title: AD - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Capital project delivery management flagged by Executive as requiring external review
findings.detail: Executive identified capital project management as an area for improvement and the Chief Executive commissioned an external review of the council's approach to managing major capital projects. Recommendations from this review will be taken forward in the coming year, indicating systematic delivery issues.
findings.matters: Poor capital governance increases risk of delays, cost overruns, and delivery failure on council infrastructure schemes
findings.figures: External review commissioned; implementation of improvements scheduled for 2026/27
findings.quote: The management of Capital Projects has been highlighted by the Executive as an area for improvement with the Chief Executive instigating an external review of the Council's approach to managing major capital project delivery

findings.paper_title: AD - Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 Report
findings.headline: Council remains reliant on exceptional financial support (capitalisation directions) through at least 2030/31
findings.detail: External auditors' 2024/25 value for money statement explicitly states the council 'remains reliant on significant Exceptional Financial Support in the form of capitalisation directions for the next 4 years to be able to balance its budget'. Despite reducing the capitalisation requirement from £570m to £395m, the council cannot achieve budget balance without government intervention.
findings.matters: Structural budget imbalance requiring multi-year government support signals material credit risk and limited financial flexibility
findings.figures: Capitalisation requirement reduced from £570m to £395m; reliant on exceptional support for next 4 years
findings.quote: the Council remains reliant on significant Exceptional Financial Support in the form of capitalisation directions for the next 4 years to be able to balance its budget and our conclusion is this is evidence of the continuing weakness in arrangements

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Financial control demonstrated with £3m underspend and £41.5m reserve increase in 2024/25
findings.detail: Despite budget pressures, the council delivered a £3m revenue underspend in 2024/25 and increased reserves by £41.5m. Capital spending was controlled at £271m (£2.1m over a £267.9m reprofiled budget). The government ended the Best Value Notice in February 2025 recognising progress made.
findings.matters: The demonstrated financial control and reserve building provides some reassurance on management quality and creates a buffer for future pressures. Ending of the Best Value Notice signals improved regulatory confidence.
findings.figures: Revenue underspend 2024/25: £3m; Reserve increase: £41.5m; Capital outturn: £271m (overspend £2.1m); Best Value Notice ended February 2025
findings.quote: The financial performance of revenue and capital budgets in 2024/25 demonstrates the grip and control the Council has developed, alongside the more accurate and realistic projections which enable close delivery of the budget through the year

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Council tax increased 9.99% for 2025/26 to reduce exceptional financial support requirement
findings.detail: The council agreed a one-off 9.99% council tax increase for 2025/26 to increase income and reduce the capitalisation direction requirement. This large increase, implemented unilaterally without a referendum, indicates significant financial pressure.
findings.matters: A 9.99% council tax increase signals substantial financial strain and indicates the council is maximizing available revenue levers to manage its funding gap.
findings.figures: Council tax increase 2025/26: 9.99%
findings.quote: The Council agreed a one off 9.99% increase in Council Tax for 2025/26 which increased the level of income it would generate in 2025/26 and hence reduced the level of CD required to plug the funding gap

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Children's Services remains inadequate with government intervention despite monitoring visit improvements
findings.detail: The council's Children's Services continues to be rated 'Inadequate' by Ofsted with government intervention in place since 2020. Three monitoring visits during 2024/25 provided positive feedback on progress, and the Department for Education recommended moving from enhanced monitoring to support through advisors. However, the overall rating and intervention status remain unchanged.
findings.matters: An inadequate rating in children's services indicates governance weakness in a critical statutory service. This reflects on the council's overall governance quality and creates regulatory risk.
findings.figures: Three monitoring visits completed 2024/25 (May 2024, February 2025, July 2025); Ofsted rating remains 'Inadequate'
findings.quote: the continued 'inadequate' rating and government intervention is evidence of a remaining significant weakness in arrangements

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Council needs to identify £50m annual savings for 2026/27-2027/28 with £6.6m still unplanned
findings.detail: The council achieved £46.7m savings in 2024/25 (the highest level ever delivered) and is forecasting all but £0.6m of the £44.8m 2025/26 target will be delivered. However, the council requires £50m savings annually from 2026/27 onwards, with only £43.4m identified as of March 2025.
findings.matters: The escalating savings requirements represent increasing delivery risk. Unidentified savings packages indicate the financial burden is being deferred and may not be achievable at the projected scale.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings delivered: £46.7m; 2025/26 target: £44.8m; 2026/27-2028 required: £50m per year; £6.6m unidentified as of March 2025
findings.quote: The Council has identified that savings of £50m each year will be required from 2026/27 to 2027/28. To identify these savings the council began work in early 2025/26. At March 2025 the Council had identified all but £6.6m of savings

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Asset disposal target cut by one-third from £150m to £100m over 4 years
findings.detail: The council revised its asset disposal target downwards from £150m to £100m at Quarter 2 2025/26 based on actual sales experience. Of 309 identified assets with estimated receipts of £83.1m, only 74 have been sold generating £22.3m to date, representing 27% achievement to date.
findings.matters: Asset sales are a key component of the council's plan to bridge its funding gap. The 33% downward revision indicates the programme will not generate expected capital receipts, leaving a larger structural funding gap.
findings.figures: Target revised from £150m to £100m; 309 assets identified with £83.1m estimated receipts; 74 assets sold for £22.3m
findings.quote: At Quarter 2 2025/26 this target was revised to £100m, based on actual disposal experience up until that point

findings.paper_title: Doc X - Appendix 3 - CBMDC Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Council remains reliant on capitalisation directions for next 4 years despite improved delivery
findings.detail: The council's Capitalisation Direction requirement increased from £573m (January 2025) to £640m, then reduced to £570m (March 2025) following a 9.99% council tax increase. The auditor concluded this continuing reliance on exceptional financial support, projected through 2029/30, represents a significant weakness in financial sustainability arrangements.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's structural budget deficit and four-year dependency on government support. This indicates the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources.
findings.figures: CD requirement increased from £573m to £640m (January 2025), later reduced to £570m (March 2025); forecast CD requirement to 2029/30
findings.quote: the Council remains reliant on significant Exceptional Financial Support in the form of capitalisation directions for the next 4 years to be able to balance its budget

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Interest rate rises pose material downside risk to affordability forecasts
findings.detail: The council's treasury advisors (MUFG) forecast interest rates will 'fall slightly' over the medium term, but the council acknowledges this is a forecast with uncertainty. Against this background the document states 'caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations'. However, if rates rise instead of falling, interest charges on new borrowing will be higher than modelled. The council has ~£132m of short-term loans (as of 31 Dec 2025) that are refinancing risk.
findings.matters: Interest rate sensitivity is material at this scale of borrowing. A 1% rise in rates across the portfolio would add £8-10m/year to interest costs when refinancing. This could push affordability ratios above sustainable levels and force service cuts.
findings.figures: Short-term loans (other LAs): £132m as of 31 Dec 2025, forecast £178m at 31 Mar 2026. Fixed rate debt: £707m. MUFG forecasts rates 'likely to fall over the medium-term'
findings.quote: Against this background and the risks within the economic forecast, caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of ~30% assumed in forecasts but 'likely to be repeated in future years'
findings.detail: The council has experienced slippage in the capital programme and has 'reshaped' it to reflect 'quarter 3 forecast spend for 2025/26 and slippage of about 30% for the next two years'. However, the document notes that 'Members will recall that capital spending plans have been reprofiled year on year and it is likely that the trend could be repeated in future years'. This suggests capital delivery is a persistent issue and forecasts may be optimistic.
findings.matters: If slippage is structural, then timing of borrowing, cash flow forecasts, and the ability to realise capital receipts are all at risk. Lenders care about whether a council can deliver on its spending plans as promised.
findings.figures: ~30% slippage assumed for next two years (2026/27, 2027/28)
findings.quote: the Council experiences slippage in the capital programme, the capital programme has been reshaped to reflect the quarter 3 forecast spend for 2025/26 and slippage of about 30% for the next two years.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Total borrowing forecast to increase 50% over next 5 years to fund capital programme, CD, and DSG
findings.detail: External borrowing (excluding PFI) is forecast to rise from £738m (2024/25) to £958m (2030/31), an increase of £220m or 30%, with additional PFI liabilities. This reflects three drivers: capital programme spending (~£25m/year average = £125m over period), Capitalisation Direction (~£300m cumulative 2023/24-2027/28, now reduced by £175m), and DSG deficit (~£119m from 2026/27). The document notes 'capital spending plans have been reprofiled year on year and it is likely that the trend could be repeated in future years'.
findings.matters: A 50% increase in debt burden in 5 years is substantial and will lock in high future interest and MRP charges. If capital programme continues to slip or DSG pressures grow, debt could rise further. Interest rate rises would amplify this burden.
findings.figures: 2024/25 borrowing £738m; 2025/26 forecast £814m; 2026/27 estimate £899m; 2030/31 estimate £958m. Total increase £220m (30% rise excluding PFI)
findings.quote: To set the forecast external borrowing shown in Table 6 above in context Chart 2 below shows that borrowing is forecast to increase, nearly 50% of the borrowing as of 31st March 2025, over the next 5 years.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Under-borrowing headroom shrinks significantly by 2027/28, limiting future fiscal flexibility
findings.detail: Bradford is currently 'under-borrowed' (existing debt £808m vs CFR of £1,189m as of 31 Dec 2025), meaning it has drawn less debt than its capital plan permits. However, this cushion shrinks as the CFR peaks in 2026/27 and borrowing increases. By 2027/28 the under-borrowing position narrows to just £20m, 'leaving little headroom'. This reduces the council's ability to borrow for unexpected capital needs or to manage timing mismatches.
findings.matters: Headroom is important for managing unexpected costs or timing issues in capital spending. Tight headroom limits financial flexibility and can force delayed projects or budget cuts if circumstances change.
findings.figures: 2024/25 under-borrowing: £176m; 2025/26 forecast: £205m; 2026/27 estimate: £128m; 2027/28: £20m; 2028/29: over-borrowed by £16m
findings.quote: the Council's borrowing remains very close to the CFR in 2027/28 leaving little headroom.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Final year of Capitalisation Direction (2026/27) but borrowing for revenue costs will continue beyond it
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is planned as the final year for capitalisation directions (reduced from originally planned c£570m to c£395m total through 2027/28), the underlying structural issue does not end. The DSG deficit (c£119m) will require borrowing from 2026/27 onwards. The document explicitly warns that the CD carries 'significant long-term financial implications, particularly in relation to borrowing costs and associated interest payments, which will place additional pressure on future years' budgets'.
findings.matters: The council was using EFS to balance revenue budgets by borrowing instead of cutting spending. Even after EFS ends, DSG deficits will require the same approach. This suggests structural unresolved spending pressures, not temporary cash flow management.
findings.figures: Capitalisation Direction reduced from c£570m to c£395m (c£175m reduction). Year 4 (2026-27) EFS request c£78m, planned as final year. DSG deficit borrowing c£119m from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.quote: This approach carries significant long-term financial implications, particularly in relation to borrowing costs and associated interest payments, which will place additional pressure on future years' budgets.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Capital financing costs consuming 14-17% of net income described as 'very challenging'
findings.detail: The council's capital financing charges (loan interest, MRP, finance and PFI payments) are forecast at 17% of net income receivable for 2025/26, reducing to around 14% in the medium term. The document explicitly states this level 'is very challenging and affordability remains a priority', and flags that improvements require both reducing the capital programme AND generating more capital receipts, 'programmes in place to deliver both' but which 'will need to be continued'.
findings.matters: 14-17% of revenue going to historic debt service is unusually high and constrains service spending. Lenders care about this ratio as it indicates how much fiscal flexibility the council retains, and a ratio this high leaves little room for interest rate rises or unexpected costs.
findings.quote: On the current trajectory the ratio is expected to remain around 14% in the medium-term which is very challenging and affordability remains a priority.

findings.paper_title: Doc Z - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Final
findings.headline: Council expected to breach prudential borrowing limits from 2028/29 to support DSG deficit
findings.detail: Bradford forecasts it will be unable to keep borrowing within the Capital Financing Requirement from 2028/29 onwards, reflecting an expected need to borrow c£119m to fund the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit. The document notes this represents borrowing to support revenue, in addition to capital costs, which is a breach of prudential rules. This threshold breach is expected to continue through to 2030/31.
findings.matters: Prudential code breaches signal structural deficits that can no longer be funded within capital-for-capital-purpose borrowing, indicating revenue sustainability risk. This is the first point where the council's forecasts show it cannot meet its own prudential indicators without additional government support or service cuts.
findings.figures: c£119m DSG deficit borrowing from 2028/29 onwards; borrowing to exceed CFR by £51m in 2029/30 and £90m in 2030/31
findings.quote: However, the Council's borrowing remains very close to the CFR in 2027/28 leaving little headroom. Furthermore, of concern is that current forecasts indicate that borrowing will exceed the CFR in 2028/29 and 2029/30, which indicates that the Council would be borrowing to support revenue, in addition to costs capitalised under the CD.

findings.paper_title: Doc Y- Budget Consultation
findings.headline: Cumulative equality impact assessment identifies 13 occasions of high disproportionate impact across the 36 budget proposals
findings.detail: The council has conducted equality impact assessments across 36 proposals (five new ones plus 31 prior decisions). The cumulative assessment identifies 13 occasions of high disproportionate impact on protected characteristics groups. Age and disability are most affected (5 high impacts each), followed by sex (3 high impacts). The council has committed to reviewing and monitoring these impacts during implementation, indicating ongoing governance risk.
findings.matters: High-impact equality assessments create legal risk under the Equality Act 2010. They also signal service reductions affecting vulnerable populations, which may be subject to legal challenge and may worsen council finances through litigation or required service restoration.
findings.figures: 13 high-impact occasions identified; age: 5 high impacts; disability: 5 high impacts; sex: 3 high impacts; total 102 impacts across all levels (13 high + 47 medium + 42 low)
findings.quote: Age and disability are identified at a high level of disproportionate impact on seven occasions in proposals including previously made decisions, age in five, and disability in five instances, respectively.

findings.paper_title: Doc Y- Budget Consultation
findings.headline: Proposed children's legal services spending cuts create documented safeguarding concerns for SEND pupils and care leavers
findings.detail: The £0.6m children's service savings include reductions in legal spending. Consultation respondents raised specific concerns that 'reductions in staff and legal services could adversely affect Care Leavers by weakening pathway planning and limiting access to legal support' and that 'SEND families may face disproportionate impacts if legal services are curtailed, as this could restrict access to statutory assessments and tribunal processes.' The council has not committed to safeguarding legal capacity.
findings.matters: Inadequate legal capacity in children's services creates risk of missed statutory duties (SEND assessments, tribunal representation), liability for care leavers, and potential legal challenge. Safeguarding failures are both financial and reputational risk.
findings.figures: £0.6m children's service savings; legal spend reduction component not separately quantified
findings.quote: Those opposing the proposal focused on safeguarding risks and the potential for deterioration in service quality—particularly for care leavers and SEND families—if posts or legal capacity are reduced. Similarly, concerns were raised that SEND families may face disproportionate impacts if legal services are curtailed, as this could restrict access to statutory assessments and tribunal processes.

findings.paper_title: Doc Y- Budget Consultation
findings.headline: Proposed £4m fee increase (40% of new savings proposals) faces 76% public opposition and uncertain delivery
findings.detail: The council proposed a 6% increase in fees and charges across services to raise £4m. Of 280 survey respondents, 212 (76%) disagreed with the proposal. Opposition was based on affordability and cost-of-living pressures. The council's departmental response does not commit to modifying the proposal, suggesting it intends to proceed despite strong public resistance. This £4m represents 40% of the £9.8m in new proposals.
findings.matters: If a major income proposal cannot be delivered due to political or public opposition, the council will miss its £60.6m savings target, triggering the debt consequence already flagged. A lender needs to assess whether income-raising measures in financially stressed councils are actually achievable or politically fragile.
findings.figures: £4m proposed increase; 76% opposition (212 of 280 respondents disagreed); 6% fee increase; 85 comments specifically citing affordability concerns
findings.quote: Seventy-six percent of respondents disagreed with the proposal, and 156 comments were made. Those opposing the proposal made 130 comments, summarised as follows: • Affordability (85 comments) was the most frequently raised issue. Respondents highlighted cost-of-living pressures, stating that a 6% increase would worsen financial hardship and was above inflation.

findings.paper_title: Doc Y- Budget Consultation
findings.headline: Council is in formal financial recovery requiring £60.6m in savings, with debt consequence if targets are missed
findings.detail: Bradford is executing a documented financial recovery plan. The council explicitly states: 'Delivering the £60.6m of proposed financial savings is key to the achievement of the Council's financial recovery plan' and warns that 'any savings under-achieved in 2026-27 would impact adversely on this position resulting in an increase in long term debt and the associated financing costs thereof.' The five new proposals in this report (£9.8m) are part of this required £60.6m total.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether the council is in financial recovery and whether it can deliver on its savings commitments. The council has explicitly linked savings delivery to future debt levels — failure to achieve the target increases long-term debt and financing costs.
findings.figures: £60.6m total savings required for 2026-27; £9.8m from five new proposals; existing deficit position requiring recovery plan
findings.quote: Delivering the £60.6m of proposed financial savings is key to the achievement of the Council's financial recovery plan. Whilst the Medium-Term Financial Strategy report sets out the impact of the proposed Local Government Finance Settlement on these plans, any savings under-achieved in 2026-27 would impact adversely on this position resulting in an increase in long term debt and the associated financing costs thereof.

findings.paper_title: Doc W - Strategic Risk Register – Quarter Two Update 2025- 26
findings.headline: Rising poverty in the district creates risk of lower council tax and business rates collection as households and businesses struggle financially.
findings.detail: The poverty risk (score 12, target 9 by March 2030) identifies specific pressure on the council's revenue collection. As more households and businesses face financial stress, the council faces increased demand on debt collection services and lower collection rates.
findings.matters: Lower collection rates directly impact the council's revenue base and cash flow, making the financial resilience challenge harder to solve.
findings.figures: Risk score 12, target 9 by 31 March 2030
findings.quote: Risk of lower collection levels of Council Tax, Business Rates and Sundry Debts, and increased resource demand on debt collection services, as households and businesses prioritise other debts.

findings.paper_title: Doc W - Strategic Risk Register – Quarter Two Update 2025- 26
findings.headline: Workforce risk actions have slipped, with some target dates moved back, though the April 2026 improvement deadline is still expected.
findings.detail: The workforce risk remains at score 9 with a target of 6 by 30 April 2026. The council acknowledges that action target dates have been pushed back. The risk covers recruitment, retention, affordability, and succession planning—all essential to delivering the financial improvement plan.
findings.matters: Workforce planning delays or unaffordable staffing structures undermine the council's ability to deliver budgeted savings and service transformation.
findings.figures: Current score 9, target 6 by 30 April 2026; some action target dates have moved back
findings.quote: Whilst completion of some of the action target dates have moved back, attainment of a target risk score of 6 is still expected by 30 April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Doc W - Strategic Risk Register – Quarter Two Update 2025- 26
findings.headline: SEND services are projected to overspend by £14m in 2025/26—the first time this risk has created a material impact on the council's finances.
findings.detail: Increased demand for Education, Health and Care Plans exceeds the Dedicated Schools Grant allocation. The paper explicitly identifies this as 'a projected impact on the Council's financial position in the coming financial year for the first time', reflecting national SEND funding pressures. The council is setting up a DSG financial board to mitigate, but the overspend is already forecast.
findings.matters: A £14m overspend is material to the council's annual budget and signals either demand-driven budget risk that may recur or need for reallocation from other services.
findings.figures: Projected overspend on overall DSG of circa £14m in 2025/26
findings.quote: There is a projected impact on the Council's financial position in the coming financial year for the first time due to a projected overspend on the overall DSG of circa £14m as a result of increased EHC Plans and insufficient funding to meet demand and needs.

findings.paper_title: Doc W - Strategic Risk Register – Quarter Two Update 2025- 26
findings.headline: Cyber security risk score doubled from 8 to 16 in six months, with human behaviour identified as the key vulnerability.
findings.detail: The major cyber attack risk has jumped to the highest level in this quarter. The council acknowledges cyber security is high-risk with staff behaviour as the primary vulnerability. Mandatory training is planned, but interim measures are needed first. The risk is rated 'Under Controlled', not 'Adequately Controlled'.
findings.matters: Cyber incidents can disable service delivery, corrupt or lose data, and prevent the council functioning—affecting both taxpayers and the council's ability to meet financial obligations.
findings.figures: Risk score increased from 8 to 16 between Q4 2024/25 and Q2 2025/26
findings.quote: The risk score has increased from 8 to 16. Cyber security risk is high, with human behaviour a key vulnerability.

findings.paper_title: Doc W - Strategic Risk Register – Quarter Two Update 2025- 26
findings.headline: Financial resilience remains at the highest risk level (16) despite a five-year improvement strategy targeting April 2030.
findings.detail: The council's current risk score for financial resilience is 16, with a target of 6 by April 2030. The paper notes progress through earlier account closures, budget savings plans, and in-year budget overachievement, but the magnitude of the challenge keeps the risk at maximum. The council must maintain this pace for four more years to achieve financial sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to understand the time horizon and effort required to move from maximum risk to acceptable levels, and the consequences if progress slows.
findings.figures: Current score 16 (maximum), target score 6, target date 01.04.2030
findings.quote: The overall position remains, because of the magnitude of the challenge, at a current score of 16, with a target of 6.

findings.paper_title: Doc U - CBMDC - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Audit work remains incomplete at report date, including property valuations and PFI/IFRS 16 implementation worth £128.9m
findings.detail: The auditors note audit work is substantially complete but multiple items remain outstanding: evidence supporting 7 of 18 property valuations; evidence for 3 of 7 investment property valuations; PFI transition to IFRS 16 with changes to the model still under review; IFRS 16 lease liabilities evidence; trial balance reconciliation; and a direct loan confirmation from another local authority. The audit will be signed off subject to satisfactory resolution of these matters.
findings.matters: Outstanding property valuations (£557m in land/buildings and £43m in investment properties) and £128.9m PFI liabilities are material to the balance sheet and borrowing position. Incomplete audit procedures at report date creates uncertainty about the accuracy of these figures until the audit is fully concluded.
findings.figures: £557m land and buildings; £43m investment properties; £128.9m PFI liabilities; evidence awaited for 7 of 18 property valuations and 3 of 7 investment property valuations
findings.quote: Our audit work is substantially complete and there are currently no matters of which we are aware that would require modification of our audit opinion, subject to the satisfactory resolution of the outstanding matters set out below.

findings.paper_title: Doc U - CBMDC - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Multiple prior-year asset accounting control recommendations remain unaddressed after repeated cycles
findings.detail: Asset register control issues persist: 756 assets with nil opening and closing balances remain on the register (down only 10 from prior year); £86k of other land and buildings continue to be held at historic cost rather than current value; and surplus assets valuation methodology issues continue, with assets valued on a 5-year rolling programme rather than at fair value as required. These recommendations have been raised in prior audits but not resolved.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to address auditor recommendations on asset accounting controls suggests either weak governance discipline or resourcing constraints, and indicates potential for asset valuations to be misstated, which is material to balance sheet accuracy and borrowing covenants.
findings.figures: £86k in historic cost holdings; 756 assets with nil balances; £120k net impact on opening gross cost and accumulated depreciation in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council have continued to follow this treatment in 2024/25. We conclude that this recommendation has not been addressed.

findings.paper_title: Doc U - CBMDC - Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements are expected to persist from prior years into 2024/25
findings.detail: The auditors state they anticipate that significant weaknesses in arrangements reported in prior years will remain weaknesses in 2024/25. The council's arrangements across financial sustainability, governance and efficiency will be detailed in the Auditor's Annual Report due by 30 November 2025. This represents a continuing governance and financial sustainability concern.
findings.matters: Persistent significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements indicate ongoing governance or financial management issues that directly affect the council's ability to manage resources and deliver services reliably, a core concern for lenders assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Details pending in Auditor's Annual Report (due 30 November 2025)
findings.quote: Based on the work undertaken to date we anticipate the significant weaknesses in arrangements reported in prior years will remain weaknesses in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Home to School Transport savings proposals cascading: £1.2m additional target following 2025/26 base budget increase
findings.detail: Base budget for home-to-school transport was increased in 2025/26 to reflect cost pressures, but the council is now finding £1.2m additional savings from the same service through policy tightening, in-house service delivery, and personal transport budgets. This suggests underlying volatility in the service and escalating cost control measures.
findings.matters: A volatile service receiving budget support then immediate cost-cutting signals either that cost pressures were overestimated or that further cuts are constrained by policy/service impact. Volatile services are signs of underlying demand or efficiency problems.
findings.figures: £1.2m savings; multiple component measures (policy adherence, local placements, digital tools, stricter controls)
findings.quote: Following an increase in the base budget in 2025/26 to recognise the estimated increased cost associated with the Home to School Transport service, recent and continuing work to review practise in this area has identified further savings of £1.2m from this budget

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Still reliant on Capitalisation Direction and working to reduce it
findings.detail: The summary statement notes the savings package will help the council 'reduce the Capitalisation Direction (CD)', an accounting flexibility permitting councils to charge capital grants and asset sales to revenue to offset deficits. CD is a crutch; the fact Bradford still needs it signals underlying revenue imbalance.
findings.matters: Capitalisation Direction masks the true underlying revenue position. A council still using CD after four years of £50m savings is not yet operationally balanced. It requires government permission to use and signals financial stress to rating agencies.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this report; referenced as item to 'reduce'
findings.quote: This sum being above the target will provide for, along with other elements of the financial strategy such as the in-year financial position, a mix of contingency for any undelivered proposals, help to mitigate any cost pressures, enable the Council to start to provide for the risks it faces and reduce the Capitalisation Direction (CD).

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Adult Social Care financial contribution threshold lowered for existing vulnerable service users
findings.detail: Discretionary buffer removed from non-residential financial assessments, phased 50% July 2025 and 50% July 2026. This is a real policy change raising care contributions for vulnerable adults already in receipt of care. Aligned with national minimum income guarantee but locally is a service user income measure, not an operational efficiency.
findings.matters: This is income generation from vulnerable service users, not cost control. It is politically fraught and depends on households accepting higher bills in a cost-of-living crisis. Equalities impact assessments are required. Reputational risk and potential legal challenge exist.
findings.figures: £5.0m saving; phased implementation July 2025 (50%) and July 2026 (50%)
findings.quote: To proceed with the implementation of the removal of the discretionary buffer in the calculation of non-residential financial assessments with the following adjustments: A phased implementation of the proposed discretionary buffer 5 removal 50% in July 2025 and 50% in July 2026 for existing services users.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Income budget assumptions (parking, theatres) rest on volatile baselines recently reset downward
findings.detail: Theatres over-achieved budget by £1.5m in 2024/25 but the council now assumes only £500k, calling 2024/25 a one-off. Parking income exceeded budget by £800k in 2024/25, with £300k assessed as one-off; the council is raising the baseline for ongoing growth. These are material income assumptions grafted onto volatile income streams.
findings.matters: A £1.5m swing in one service (theatres) shows income is uncontrollable. If 2024/25 was not one-off, or if parking growth does not materialise, these income assumptions fail silently. Income slippage and revenue shortfalls are a traditional cause of unexpected borrowing.
findings.figures: Theatres £1.5m over-achieve in 2024/25, budgeted to £500k from 2026/27; parking income exceeded by £800k in 2024/25
findings.quote: In 2024/25, Theatres over-achieved their budget by £1.5m. In recent years, prior to 2024/25, the over achievement of income was around £500k per year. It is accepted that performance in 2024/25 was a one-off, due to programming, and not part of a trend, meaning that 2024/25 performance levels are not likely to be repeated.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Still in year 4 of 7-year recovery plan with £50m annual savings requirement through 2029/30
findings.detail: Bradford was placed on enhanced oversight and required to find £50m savings each year until the end of 2029/30 to reach financial sustainability. This year's £60.6m is above target and provides modest headroom, but three more years of equivalent savings still lie ahead. The council explicitly states major challenges remain.
findings.matters: This is not a one-year trough; this is mid-cycle in a multi-year structural adjustment. Lenders need to know the council is four-fifths through, not one-fifth through. Any slip in annual delivery accumulates risk in the out-years.
findings.figures: Year 4 of 7-year plan; £50m annual requirement through 2029/30; £60.6m proposed for 2026/27
findings.quote: These proposed savings will be the fourth year's contribution to the 7 year recovery period.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: £7.2m pension contribution saving is structural but non-repeatable
findings.detail: West Yorkshire Pension Fund has notified the council that employer contributions will reduce from 16.2% to 12.3%. This is a genuine recurring saving, not a one-off, but it is driven by actuary decisions outside the council's control and cannot be repeated.
findings.matters: This is a material windfall (12% of the total £60.6m package). It improves the baseline but masks underlying operational delivery risk. Lenders assess recurring operational sustainability, not pension actuarial changes.
findings.figures: £7.2m saving; reduction from 16.2% to 12.3% contribution rate
findings.quote: The Council has recently received notice of a proposed reduction from next financial year in its' employer pension contributions to the West Yorkshire Pension Fund from 16.2% to 12.3%. BCFT contributions are also reducing from 15.2% to 12.3%. The cumulative financial benefit of this to the Council's budget position is £7.2m.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: £5m turnover savings assumption sits atop £11m prior-year underspend
findings.detail: The council is targeting £5m in vacancy/turnover savings for 2026/27, relying on holding staff vacancies. This comes after departments underspent by £11m in 2024/25 and forecast £6m in 2025/26, suggesting either that posts are hard to fill or that turnover assumptions are proving optimistic.
findings.matters: Turnover is unpredictable and volatile. If posts fill faster than assumed, this £5m saving will not materialise. For a council running a 7-year recovery plan, a £5m miss on uncontrollable turnover is material.
findings.figures: £5m savings target; £11m underspend 2024/25; £6m forecast 2025/26
findings.quote: Turnover across the Council. Council departments underspent by £11m in 2024-25, and a further c£6m is forecast in 2025-26.

findings.paper_title: Doc O- 2026- 27 Revenue Budget Savings Proposals
findings.headline: Adult Social Care workforce restructuring with 26 identified redundancies
findings.detail: The council has issued formal redundancy notices (S188 letters to trade unions and HR1 to government on 13 October 2025) for 26 posts in Adult Social Care. The restructuring is designed to transform service delivery but places this critical social care workforce in flux.
findings.matters: ASC is a protected statutory service and a major budget area; workforce instability during transformation affects service continuity. Redundancy execution risk is material, and service delivery during transition is uncertain.
findings.figures: 26 employees directly impacted; ASC proposals total £4.0m of £60.6m savings
findings.quote: Twenty six Council employees have been identified as directly impacted by the Adult Social Care budget proposals for 2026-27 and therefore may be at risk of redundancy (as defined under section 195 TULRCA 1992.) A HR1 form to Government and a S188 letter to the recognised Trade Unions detailing which posts are at risk of redundancy was issued on 13 October 2025.

news_drafts.headline: SCAPE discount rate increase has suspended critical pension calculations pending new actuarial factors, extending timelines by up to six months
news_drafts.lead: Suspended transfer-out processing creates bottlenecks affecting member and employer experience; delays in member valuations disrupt retirement planning for members and inter-fund administration

news_drafts.headline: Internal audit rated life certificate controls as only partially effective, finding multiple risks not effectively managed
news_drafts.lead: Weakness in life certificate controls creates risk of overpayments to deceased pensioners; as a material process in pension administration, control failures here expose Bradford to financial loss and regulatory scrutiny

news_drafts.headline: WYPF will breach McCloud statutory guidance by failing to complete retrospective pension amendments by 31 August 2026
news_drafts.lead: Breaching Pensions Regulator requirements can result in fines and regulatory action; as Bradford hosts WYPF, this compliance failure reflects on Bradford's governance and ability to manage complex regulatory obligations
